# Instructions

Compute the result for a game of Hex / Polygon.

The abstract boardgame known as [Hex][hex] / Polygon / CON-TAC-TIX is quite simple in rules, though complex in practice.
Two players place stones on a parallelogram with hexagonal fields.
The player to connect his/her stones to the opposite side first wins.
The four sides of the parallelogram are divided between the two players (i.e. one player gets assigned a side and the side directly opposite it and the other player gets assigned the two other sides).

Your goal is to build a program that given a simple representation of a board computes the winner (or lack thereof).
Note that all games need not be "fair".
(For example, players may have mismatched piece counts or the game's board might have a different width and height.)

The boards look like this:

```text
. O . X .
 . X X O .
  O O O X .
   . X O X O
    X O O O X
```

"Player `O`" plays from top to bottom, "Player `X`" plays from left to right.
In the above example `O` has made a connection from left to right but nobody has won since `O` didn't connect top and bottom.

[hex]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hex_%28board_game%29

Use the instructions above to complete `connect.py`. Keep the existing function and class names: tests you cannot see import them. Use only the Python standard library.

{"content":"# Hex / Polygon

## Python solver

`ConnectGame(board).get_winner()` returns `"X"` for a left-to-right connection,
`"O"` for a top-to-bottom connection, or `""` for neither.
The input is a multiline string of X, O and . cells. Whitespace is ignored.
Rectangular boards and unequal stone counts are supported.

Run tests with `python -m unittest discover -v`.

## Browser companion

Build with `python build_web.py`, then open `dist/index.html` in a browser.
No dependencies, server or network access are required.

Click or tap an empty hex to place a stone, alternating X and O. Keyboard users
can use Tab and Enter. The game stops when a player connects their assigned
sides; New game resets the board. The separate text checker accepts rectangular
boards, including positions with unequal piece counts. Nothing is persisted.

The browser companion implements the same six-neighbor search in JavaScript;
it does not execute Python. `connect.py` remains the Python exercise entry point.

### Design and assets

A compact 3×3 local two-player game makes connections easy to explore. A separate
checker handles larger supplied positions. Letters distinguish players as well
as colors. Narrow screens stack the panels. All visuals are original CSS and
system text; there are no external images, fonts, audio or other assets.

See `artifacts/final-evidence.md` for verification status.
